course.title: Incident Response
course.description: A research-based cybersecurity incident-response course that teaches students how to prepare for, detect, triage, investigate, contain, eradicate, recover from, document, and learn from security incidents. The course uses current NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 and NIST CSF 2.0 concepts, FIRST CSIRT practices, CISA operational guidance, NIST forensic and recovery guidance, MITRE ATT&CK for behavioral analysis, and cloud-provider incident-response principles. Students practice evidence-based decision making, timeline analysis, evidence integrity, ransomware response, communications, metrics, safe automation, and a complete simulated end-to-end incident.
prerequisites: basic computer and operating-system administration knowledge
basic TCP/IP networking and authentication concepts
basic cybersecurity concepts such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, vulnerabilities, logs, and indicators of compromise
ability to use a command line at a basic level
Python 3 familiarity is helpful for automation exercises but not required for conceptual lessons
learningOutcomes: explain modern incident-response terminology, governance, roles, and lifecycle concepts
map incident-response activities to NIST CSF 2.0 and SP 800-61 Rev. 3
design response readiness plans covering people, process, technology, access, evidence, and exercises
triage security alerts using evidence, scope, confidence, and business context
construct incident timelines from heterogeneous identity, endpoint, network, application, and cloud telemetry
investigate account compromise and endpoint/network activity using hypothesis-driven analysis
select and verify proportionate containment and eradication actions
handle ransomware scenarios with evidence preservation, recovery prioritization, and communication controls
apply NIST SP 800-86 concepts for evidence collection, examination, analysis, reporting, and integrity verification
create evidence registers, hashes, case records, and defensible incident reports
design incident communications, response metrics, lessons-learned reviews, and improvement backlogs
adapt incident response to cloud environments and design safe, auditable automation
complete an end-to-end simulated incident-response case from initial alert through closure and continuous improvement

modules.title: Incident Response Foundations and Governance
modules.description: Build the mental model, terminology, governance, roles, scope, and risk-based decision-making needed before technical response begins.

lessons.title: What Incident Response Is and Is Not
lessons.description: Define cybersecurity incident response, distinguish events from incidents, and understand why response is a risk-management capability rather than a single technical tool.
learningObjectives: explain the difference between an event, alert, incident, and major incident
describe the purpose of incident response in organizational risk management
distinguish incident response from business continuity, disaster recovery, vulnerability management, and threat hunting
identify the lifecycle activities that recur throughout a response

notes.text: Core distinction

An event is an observable occurrence; an alert is a notification generated by a detection mechanism; an incident is an occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes confidentiality, integrity, availability, or other organizational security objectives and requires response. The exact declaration threshold belongs to organizational policy and risk tolerance.

items: Incident response is broader than malware removal.
Response decisions should be driven by impact, scope, confidence, and business context.
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 is the current NIST incident-response guidance and supersedes Rev. 2.
Response is continuous and iterative; investigation can change containment and recovery decisions.

notes.text: Do not treat every security alert as a confirmed incident. Premature declaration can waste scarce response capacity, while delayed declaration can increase harm.

practicals.title: Classify security observations
practicals.description: Classify sample observations as event, alert, suspected incident, confirmed incident, or non-security operational issue and justify the decision.
steps: Create a table with columns: observation, evidence, classification, confidence, next action.
Classify at least six observations such as repeated failed logins, an EDR malware alert, an approved administrator change, and an unusual outbound connection.
For each suspected or confirmed incident, state what additional evidence would change your confidence.
Review whether the proposed classification follows an explicit organizational threshold rather than personal intuition.
practicals.solution: Use a decision table that records the observation, available evidence, confidence, and required next action before assigning a final classification.
practicals.output: The completed table shows defensible classifications and explicitly identifies uncertainty and evidence gaps.

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Every alert is a confirmed incident.
Incident response is only malware removal.
Incident response uses evidence and risk context to decide how to handle potentially harmful activity.
Recovery eliminates the need for investigation.
quiz.answer: Incident response uses evidence and risk context to decide how to handle potentially harmful activity.
quiz.explanation: A response process evaluates evidence, impact, scope, and organizational context; an alert alone does not establish a confirmed incident.

summary: Incident response is a coordinated risk-management capability, not a single product.
Clear terminology prevents analysts from treating alerts, incidents, and operational issues as interchangeable.

lessons.title: NIST CSF 2.0 and the Modern IR Lifecycle
lessons.description: Map incident response to NIST CSF 2.0 and understand how Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover work as concurrent functions.
learningObjectives: explain the six NIST CSF 2.0 Functions
map preparation, detection, response, and recovery activities to CSF outcomes
explain why incident response is not isolated to the Respond Function
use CSF terminology to communicate response capability to technical and nontechnical stakeholders

notes.text: Six concurrent Functions

items: Govern establishes strategy, policy, roles, oversight, and risk context.
Identify develops understanding of assets, risks, and dependencies.
Protect establishes safeguards that reduce likelihood or impact.
Detect finds and analyzes possible cybersecurity threats and events.
Respond manages detected incidents and their effects.
Recover restores assets and operations and communicates recovery activities.

notes.text: NIST CSF 2.0 treats the Functions as concurrent and continuous. SP 800-61 Rev. 3 integrates incident response considerations into cybersecurity risk management rather than presenting response as a standalone sequence that begins only after compromise.

practicals.title: Map an incident process to CSF 2.0
practicals.description: Build a CSF 2.0 mapping for a fictional account-compromise response.
steps: List preparation activities such as asset inventory, logging, contact lists, and exercises.
List detection and analysis activities such as alert validation, scoping, and timeline construction.
List containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons-learned activities.
Map each activity to one or more CSF Functions and explain why the mapping is useful.
practicals.solution: Create a mapping table rather than forcing every activity into exactly one Function; CSF Functions can be related and concurrent.
practicals.output: A completed mapping demonstrates that preparation and recovery are as important to response capability as the immediate technical response.

quiz.question: How does CSF 2.0 characterize its six Functions?
options: As a strictly linear six-step incident workflow
As concurrent and continuous Functions for managing cybersecurity risk
As six vendor-specific tools
As mandatory phases that replace organizational procedures
quiz.answer: As concurrent and continuous Functions for managing cybersecurity risk
quiz.explanation: NIST describes Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover as concurrent and continuous Functions.

summary: CSF 2.0 provides a common language for outcomes and risk communication.
SP 800-61 Rev. 3 aligns incident-response recommendations with CSF 2.0.

lessons.title: CSIRT Roles, RACI, and Escalation
lessons.description: Design an incident-response operating model with clear technical, business, legal, communications, and executive responsibilities.
learningObjectives: describe common CSIRT functions and stakeholders
create a simple RACI matrix for a security incident
define escalation triggers based on impact, uncertainty, and business criticality
identify why out-of-band communications and predefined contacts matter

notes.text: FIRST describes CSIRTs as capabilities that provide services and support to a defined constituency. A response capability can be centralized, distributed, virtual, or embedded, but it needs a clear mandate, governance model, services, and processes.

items: Incident commander or coordinator: drives decisions, priorities, and synchronization.
Technical responders: investigate, contain, eradicate, and recover systems.
IT/service owners: provide system context and execute approved operational changes.
Legal/privacy/compliance: advise on obligations, evidence handling, contracts, and notifications.
Communications: manages internal/external messaging and reduces contradictory statements.
Executive/business owners: make risk, continuity, and resource decisions.

notes.text: Do not assume a technical responder is authorized to make legal, regulatory, employment, or public-disclosure decisions.

practicals.title: Build an incident RACI
practicals.description: Create a RACI matrix for a suspected data-exfiltration incident.
steps: Define roles for incident lead, SOC analyst, system owner, identity administrator, legal/privacy, communications, executive sponsor, and external responder.
Assign Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed roles for triage, evidence preservation, containment, notification assessment, and recovery.
Identify at least two escalation conditions.
Check for conflicting Accountable assignments and resolve them.
practicals.solution: Use one accountable decision owner per activity, while allowing multiple responsible or consulted roles where justified.
practicals.output: The RACI identifies ownership and reduces delays caused by unclear authority.

quiz.question: Why is an explicit escalation model important?
options: It eliminates the need for evidence.
It ensures every analyst can make every organizational decision.
It defines when and how incidents move to higher authority or specialized support.
It guarantees that incidents are never severe.
quiz.answer: It defines when and how incidents move to higher authority or specialized support.
quiz.explanation: Escalation provides a predictable route for decisions requiring broader authority, specialized expertise, or additional resources.

summary: A CSIRT needs a mandate and defined services, not merely a toolset.
RACI clarifies ownership while escalation criteria connect technical findings to organizational decisions.

lessons.title: Policies, Playbooks, Runbooks, and Case Records
lessons.description: Distinguish policy, plan, playbook, runbook, checklist, and case documentation, and design response documentation that remains useful during stress.
learningObjectives: differentiate governance documents from operational procedures
identify the minimum information a case record should capture
write an actionable incident playbook step
explain why timestamps, decision rationale, and evidence references matter

items: Policy states organizational intent and authority.
Plan describes how the organization organizes incident response.
Playbook describes a repeatable response pattern for a scenario or incident class.
Runbook gives technical, often tool-specific execution steps.
Checklist reduces omission risk during stressful response.
Case record preserves the evolving facts, decisions, actions, owners, timestamps, and evidence references.

notes.text: Good response documentation is operational rather than decorative. A responder who takes over a case should be able to understand what is known, what is uncertain, what has been done, what must not be done, and who owns the next decision.

practicals.title: Write a phishing-response playbook excerpt
practicals.description: Create a concise playbook section that a SOC analyst can execute after a malicious email is reported.
steps: Define initial validation questions and evidence to collect.
Define containment actions such as disabling a compromised session or removing malicious messages when authorized.
Define scoping questions for other recipients and endpoints.
Define escalation and closure criteria.
Include explicit notes for evidence preservation and documentation.
practicals.solution: Write the playbook as ordered actions with decision points, ownership, prerequisites, and stop conditions rather than prose alone.
practicals.output: The playbook is executable by another trained analyst and produces a consistent case record.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a runbook?
options: Define organizational risk appetite
Provide executable technical steps for a known operational scenario
Replace legal review
Store raw forensic images
quiz.answer: Provide executable technical steps for a known operational scenario
quiz.explanation: A runbook operationalizes a repeatable procedure, often with concrete commands, tool actions, prerequisites, and verification steps.

summary: Operational documents should separate authority and intent from technical execution.
Case records must preserve chronology, decisions, ownership, and evidence references.

tasks.title: Design a small CSIRT operating model
tasks.description: Design a lightweight incident-response capability for a 200-person organization.
tasks.problemStatement: The organization has no formal IR process, a small IT team, centralized identity, endpoint protection, and cloud-hosted email. Create a practical operating model that can handle account compromise, malware, and data-loss incidents.
objectives: select core services and response capabilities
requirements: A text editor or spreadsheet for the RACI
tasks.hint: Start from required services and decision authority, then select tools that support those services.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution models the operating capability explicitly: roles are mapped to responsibilities, and organizational decisions are separated from technical execution. The student should turn this model into a RACI and escalation matrix rather than treating the Python snippet itself as the deliverable.

modules.title: Preparation, Telemetry, and Detection Readiness
modules.description: Prepare the organization to detect and investigate incidents by establishing telemetry, access, evidence sources, contacts, exercises, and readiness checks.

lessons.title: Preparation and Readiness Engineering
lessons.description: Build a preparation checklist that addresses people, process, technology, access, evidence, dependencies, and exercises.
learningObjectives: identify preparation controls that materially reduce response time
design a responder-access strategy with least privilege and emergency access
explain why response tooling should be prepared before an incident
design a readiness test that verifies more than documentation

items: People: roles, contacts, training, on-call coverage, surge support.
Process: plans, playbooks, severity, escalation, evidence handling, notification paths.
Technology: endpoint visibility, centralized logs, identity telemetry, network visibility, backup/recovery tooling.
Access: responder permissions, break-glass procedures, MFA, out-of-band communication.
Exercises: tabletop exercises, technical simulations, recovery tests, lessons learned.

notes.text: Preparation is a measurable capability. A plan that exists but cannot be accessed, exercised, or executed under pressure is not equivalent to a tested response capability.

practicals.title: Run a readiness gap assessment
practicals.description: Assess a fictional organization against a practical incident-response readiness checklist.
steps: Create categories for people, process, technology, access, evidence, and recovery.
For each category, mark capability as ready, partial, or missing.
Prioritize gaps using business impact and response dependency.
Write three remediation actions that can be tested within 30 days.
practicals.solution: Score capabilities qualitatively and attach a verification method to every claimed capability, such as a test call, log query, access test, or exercise.
practicals.output: The output is a prioritized readiness backlog with measurable verification methods.

quiz.question: Which readiness measure is strongest?
options: A plan stored in an inaccessible folder
A contact list never tested
A documented and exercised procedure with verified responder access
A tool purchased but never configured
quiz.answer: A documented and exercised procedure with verified responder access
quiz.explanation: Effective preparation requires both documentation and demonstrated operational capability.

summary: Preparation reduces response friction before the first alert.
Readiness claims should be verified through tests and exercises.

lessons.title: Logging, Telemetry, and Evidence Sources
lessons.description: Understand the role of endpoint, identity, network, application, cloud, and authentication logs in incident investigation.
learningObjectives: categorize common telemetry sources
explain why time synchronization and retention matter
identify gaps created by incomplete logging
select high-value telemetry for a given incident hypothesis

notes.text: Logs are records of events produced by systems and services. Effective incident response requires sufficient coverage, trustworthy timestamps, appropriate retention, protected storage, and usable access. NIST log-management guidance emphasizes generating, transmitting, storing, accessing, and disposing of logs as a lifecycle.

items: Identity logs can show authentication, privilege changes, MFA events, and session context.
Endpoint telemetry can show processes, files, persistence, and security-control events.
Network telemetry can show connections, DNS activity, proxy events, and firewall decisions.
Application logs can expose authentication, authorization, errors, and transaction context.
Cloud audit logs can record control-plane activity and resource changes.

notes.text: A log source is only useful if responders can retrieve it, interpret it, and trust its integrity and time context.

practicals.title: Build a telemetry matrix
practicals.description: Choose telemetry sources for three hypotheses: stolen credentials, malware execution, and unauthorized cloud-resource change.
steps: Create rows for identity, endpoint, network, application, cloud control-plane, and storage logs.
For each hypothesis, identify primary and supporting telemetry.
Identify retention and access risks.
Explain which missing source would most weaken the investigation.
practicals.solution: Rank telemetry by evidentiary value and availability for the specific hypothesis instead of listing every possible log source.
practicals.output: The matrix demonstrates hypothesis-driven collection and exposes visibility gaps.

quiz.question: Why is time synchronization important during incident response?
options: It makes malware harmless.
It lets analysts correlate events across systems into a defensible timeline.
It eliminates the need for log retention.
It replaces host forensics.
quiz.answer: It lets analysts correlate events across systems into a defensible timeline.
quiz.explanation: Accurate and comparable timestamps are essential for reconstructing sequences across hosts, identities, applications, and network devices.

summary: Telemetry should be selected according to investigation questions and risk.
Centralized, protected, time-consistent logs improve correlation and retrospective analysis.

lessons.title: Alert Triage and Signal Validation
lessons.description: Learn how to validate alerts, suppress obvious benign activity without losing visibility, and decide when to escalate.
learningObjectives: distinguish alert fidelity from incident severity
validate an alert using independent evidence
record confidence and uncertainty
avoid confirmation bias during triage

notes.text: Triage is a decision process, not simply sorting alerts by vendor severity. Analysts should validate the alert source, affected entities, observed behavior, expected context, and corroborating evidence before deciding whether to escalate.

items: Confirm the alert is technically plausible.
Identify affected users, hosts, accounts, services, and time window.
Seek corroborating telemetry.
Check authorized activity and known maintenance windows.
Estimate scope and potential impact.
Escalate or close with documented rationale.

practicals.title: Triage a suspicious authentication alert
practicals.description: Analyze a supplied set of fictional authentication records and decide whether the alert warrants escalation.
steps: Group authentication events by account and source.
Compare successful and failed logins within a defined time window.
Look for unusual geography, device, or authentication-method changes.
Write a triage conclusion with confidence and next evidence to collect.
practicals.solution:
from collections import defaultdict

events = [
    {"user":"analyst1","src":"198.51.100.20","result":"failure","time":"09:01"},
    {"user":"analyst1","src":"198.51.100.20","result":"failure","time":"09:02"},
    {"user":"analyst1","src":"198.51.100.20","result":"success","time":"09:03"},
    {"user":"analyst1","src":"203.0.113.50","result":"success","time":"09:20"},
]
by_user = defaultdict(list)
for e in events:
    by_user[e["user"]].append(e)

for user, rows in by_user.items():
    failures = sum(r["result"] == "failure" for r in rows)
    successes = sum(r["result"] == "success" for r in rows)
    sources = sorted({r["src"] for r in rows})
    print(user, {"failures": failures, "successes": successes, "sources": sources})
practicals.output: The code demonstrates grouping and simple evidence extraction, but it does not make the incident decision automatically. The analyst must interpret the result, validate the second source, and consider whether the activity is authorized.

quiz.question: What is the strongest triage conclusion?
options: The vendor severity alone proves compromise.
The alert is ignored because one event was expected.
The alert is evaluated with corroborating evidence, scope, and confidence before escalation.
Every failed login is an incident.
quiz.answer: The alert is evaluated with corroborating evidence, scope, and confidence before escalation.
quiz.explanation: Triage requires validation and context rather than relying on one signal or a single severity label.

summary: Triage converts raw alerts into defensible response decisions.
Confidence and uncertainty should be recorded explicitly.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence and ATT&CK for Investigation
lessons.description: Use threat intelligence and MITRE ATT&CK as analytic context without treating technique labels as proof of attribution.
learningObjectives: explain the role of ATT&CK tactics and techniques in investigation
map observed behaviors to plausible ATT&CK concepts
use intelligence to generate hypotheses and enrichment
distinguish behavior mapping from actor attribution

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK organizes adversary behavior into tactics and techniques. In incident response, ATT&CK can help analysts describe what happened, identify likely next behaviors, and select detection or containment opportunities.

items: A technique mapping is an analytic description, not proof of who performed the activity.
Use observed evidence first; then map behavior to ATT&CK.
Threat intelligence is useful when it changes a decision, search, prioritization, or containment action.
Avoid copying indicators into cases without recording provenance and confidence.

practicals.title: Map behaviors to ATT&CK
practicals.description: Map a short fictional attack narrative to relevant ATT&CK tactics and techniques and identify investigative questions.
steps: Extract concrete behaviors from the narrative without guessing the actor.
Map each behavior to a plausible ATT&CK technique or sub-technique.
For each mapping, identify one telemetry source that could validate it.
Identify one containment or detection improvement suggested by the mapping.
practicals.solution: Use the MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise knowledge base to validate technique names and IDs; do not infer attribution from the mapping.
practicals.output: The result is a behavior-centric investigation plan with evidence requirements.

quiz.question: What does an ATT&CK technique mapping establish?
options: The exact identity of the attacker
A guaranteed malware family
A structured description of an observed or hypothesized adversary behavior
A legal conclusion
quiz.answer: A structured description of an observed or hypothesized adversary behavior
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK describes adversary behavior; it does not by itself establish attribution.

summary: ATT&CK is valuable for describing behavior, hypotheses, and detection opportunities.
Attribution requires additional evidence and should not be inferred from technique overlap alone.

tasks.title: Build a telemetry and readiness plan
tasks.description: Create a readiness plan for a hybrid organization that must investigate identity compromise and ransomware.
tasks.problemStatement: The organization has endpoints, centralized identity, SaaS email, a small cloud footprint, and limited SOC staffing. Build a 90-day plan covering telemetry, access, retention, contacts, and exercises.
objectives: define responder access and evidence retrieval
define two exercises and their success criteria
tasks.hint: Prioritize the capabilities that shorten time-to-understand and time-to-contain, not the largest possible tool inventory.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan is organized around measurable readiness outcomes. The student should attach owners, dependencies, and verification evidence to each action.

modules.title: Investigation, Scoping, and Timeline Analysis
modules.description: Turn alerts and artifacts into an evidence-based incident picture using hypotheses, scoping, timelines, identity analysis, and endpoint/network investigation.

lessons.title: Investigation Hypotheses and Scope
lessons.description: Develop explicit investigation questions and scope an incident without prematurely assuming the root cause.
learningObjectives: formulate testable investigation hypotheses
define scope dimensions such as users, hosts, accounts, time, data, and services
separate confirmed facts from hypotheses
build a scope matrix that tracks evidence and confidence

notes.text: An investigation is stronger when analysts state what they are trying to establish. Useful hypotheses are falsifiable: for example, “the compromised identity was used to access service X between 09:00 and 11:00” can be tested against authentication and service logs.

items: Scope horizontally across identities, endpoints, network, cloud, applications, and data.
Scope temporally using a known earliest and latest plausible time.
Scope by business impact as well as technical reach.
Record evidence that supports, weakens, or leaves each hypothesis unresolved.

practicals.title: Create an incident scope matrix
practicals.description: Build a scope matrix for a suspected compromised identity.
steps: Create rows for users, endpoints, source IPs, sessions, applications, data stores, and cloud resources.
For each entity, record status: confirmed, suspected, cleared, or unknown.
Attach the evidence source and timestamp range.
Identify the highest-priority unknown that could change containment.
practicals.solution: Keep unknowns visible rather than converting them into “not affected” without evidence.
practicals.output: The matrix becomes a living scope artifact that can be updated as evidence changes.

quiz.question: Why should investigators keep unknowns explicit?
options: Unknown means compromised.
Unknown means safe.
Unknown identifies an evidence gap that may affect scope or response decisions.
Unknown should be deleted from the case.
quiz.answer: Unknown identifies an evidence gap that may affect scope or response decisions.
quiz.explanation: Explicit uncertainty prevents false confidence and directs additional collection.

summary: Good scoping is iterative and evidence-driven.
A scope matrix helps prevent “not observed” from being mistaken for “not affected.”

lessons.title: Timeline Construction and Correlation
lessons.description: Construct a normalized incident timeline and correlate events across multiple sources.
learningObjectives: normalize timestamps and time zones
sort heterogeneous events into a timeline
identify causal relationships cautiously
use timeline gaps to direct additional collection

notes.text: Timeline analysis combines heterogeneous observations into a chronological view. Analysts should preserve original timestamps and record any conversion to a common time basis.

Example normalized record:
2026-09-07T09:14:22Z | identity | user=analyst1 | login=success | src=203.0.113.50
2026-09-07T09:16:04Z | endpoint | host=WS-07 | process=powershell.exe | parent=explorer.exe
Chronological order does not prove causation. Correlation should be supported by additional evidence such as process lineage, authentication context, network connections, or file artifacts.

practicals.title: Normalize a multi-source timeline
practicals.description: Merge identity, endpoint, and network events into a common UTC timeline.
steps: Parse timestamps from each source.
Convert them to UTC while preserving the original timestamp in the record.
Sort events by timestamp.
Add a source field and correlation key where appropriate.
Write two cautious observations and one unresolved question.
practicals.solution:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

records = [
    {"time":"2026-09-07T09:16:04+00:00","source":"endpoint","event":"powershell-start"},
    {"time":"2026-09-07T09:14:22+00:00","source":"identity","event":"login-success"},
    {"time":"2026-09-07T09:17:11+00:00","source":"network","event":"dns-query"},
]
for r in sorted(records, key=lambda x: datetime.fromisoformat(x["time"])):
    print(r["time"], r["source"], r["event"])
practicals.output: The example performs deterministic timestamp sorting. A real investigation must also preserve raw records and document time-zone assumptions.

quiz.question: What should a timeline preserve?
options: Only converted timestamps
Original evidence plus normalized time representation and source context
Only analyst conclusions
Only vendor severity
quiz.answer: Original evidence plus normalized time representation and source context
quiz.explanation: Preserving source context and original values supports repeatability and later verification.

summary: Timeline construction supports correlation but does not by itself prove causation.
Normalization should preserve original evidence and document time assumptions.

lessons.title: Identity and Account Compromise Investigation
lessons.description: Investigate credential misuse, session anomalies, privilege changes, and persistence while minimizing disruption.
learningObjectives: investigate suspicious authentication sequences
correlate identity activity with endpoint and application telemetry
identify privilege changes and persistence indicators
choose containment actions appropriate to account scope

items: Review authentication method, source, device, time, application, and success/failure context.
Investigate MFA changes, new authentication methods, token/session anomalies, and privilege assignments where telemetry supports them.
Check whether suspicious activity is consistent with approved travel, automation, service accounts, or administrative work.
Containment may include session revocation, credential reset, token invalidation, or temporary account restriction depending on the identity system and organizational procedure.

notes.text: Resetting credentials too early can destroy useful investigative context or alert an adversary. Coordinate containment with evidence-preservation needs and the risk of continued compromise.

practicals.title: Investigate a suspected account takeover
practicals.description: Analyze a fictional sequence of authentication and privilege events and produce a containment recommendation.
steps: Build a timeline for the account.
Identify unusual source, device, authentication, and privilege changes.
Cross-check endpoint or application evidence where available.
Recommend the least disruptive containment action that reduces current risk.
Document what evidence should be preserved before the action.
practicals.solution: Use the account timeline to distinguish suspicious activity from confirmed compromise and explain the trade-off between immediate containment and evidence preservation.
practicals.output: The output is a defensible account-compromise assessment with a documented containment decision.

quiz.question: What is a useful first step when investigating account compromise?
options: Assume every login is malicious
Correlate authentication context with device, application, and privilege activity
Delete all account logs
Immediately shut down every system
quiz.answer: Correlate authentication context with device, application, and privilege activity
quiz.explanation: Correlation helps determine whether authentication activity is suspicious and how far the compromise may extend.

summary: Identity investigation combines authentication, session, privilege, endpoint, and application context.
Containment should be risk-based and coordinated with evidence needs.

lessons.title: Endpoint and Network Investigation
lessons.description: Investigate process execution, persistence, files, network connections, DNS, and security-control telemetry in a controlled manner.
learningObjectives: identify high-value endpoint artifacts
use process and network relationships to expand or narrow scope
recognize common persistence categories without assuming compromise
collect volatile information when justified by the case

notes.text: Endpoint and network investigation should be hypothesis-driven. Useful questions include: what executed, under which identity, from which parent process, with what files, and which network destinations were contacted?

items: Windows: security/application/system logs, PowerShell logging where configured, services, scheduled tasks, registry persistence, process telemetry.
Linux: auth logs, systemd/service state, shell history when appropriate, process state, network sockets, cron/systemd timers.
Network: DNS, proxy, firewall, flow, VPN, and authentication telemetry.
Collect volatile data when its loss would materially affect the investigation and when authorized.

practicals.title: Build an endpoint triage checklist
practicals.description: Create a host triage checklist that can be used before deeper forensic acquisition.
steps: Define host identity and current user context.
Capture running processes and network connections using approved administrative tooling.
Identify persistence locations appropriate to the operating system.
Collect relevant security logs and hashes for suspicious files.
Record commands, timestamps, operator, and output locations.
practicals.solution: Use native tools where practical and preserve command output as case evidence. Do not modify or delete suspicious artifacts during initial triage.
practicals.output: The checklist produces repeatable triage evidence while minimizing unnecessary changes to the host.

quiz.question: Why record the commands and timestamps used during triage?
options: To make the incident look larger
To support repeatability and explain how evidence was obtained
To replace evidence integrity checks
To avoid documenting results
quiz.answer: To support repeatability and explain how evidence was obtained
quiz.explanation: Documentation of acquisition actions supports repeatability, review, and defensible interpretation.

summary: Endpoint and network investigation should connect processes, identities, files, and communications.
Triage should be repeatable and minimally invasive where deeper forensic preservation is required.

tasks.title: Investigate and scope a multi-host compromise
tasks.description: Produce an evidence-based incident assessment from identity, endpoint, and network records.
tasks.problemStatement: You receive fictional CSV-like records showing a suspicious login, a PowerShell process, DNS activity, and a privilege change. Determine affected entities, build a timeline, identify evidence gaps, and recommend containment.
requirements: The lesson concepts and NIST SP 800-61/SP 800-86
tasks.hint: Do not infer causation solely from timestamp proximity. Require at least two independent evidence relationships for high-confidence claims.
tasks.solutionCode:
from datetime import datetime

records = [
    ("2026-09-07T09:14:22+00:00", "identity", "analyst1", "login success from 203.0.113.50"),
    ("2026-09-07T09:16:04+00:00", "endpoint", "WS-07", "powershell.exe started"),
    ("2026-09-07T09:17:11+00:00", "network", "WS-07", "DNS query for suspicious.example"),
    ("2026-09-07T09:22:45+00:00", "identity", "analyst1", "privilege assignment observed"),
]
for ts, source, entity, event in sorted(records, key=lambda r: datetime.fromisoformat(r[0])):
    print(ts, source, entity, event)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The code creates a reproducible baseline timeline. The final assessment must add evidence quality, scope, gaps, and response decisions rather than treating the script output as a complete investigation.

modules.title: Containment, Eradication, and Malware/Ransomware Response
modules.description: Make controlled response decisions, contain affected assets, eradicate persistence, and handle ransomware scenarios without destroying evidence or causing unnecessary business harm.

lessons.title: Containment Strategy and Decision-Making
lessons.description: Choose containment actions based on scope, business criticality, adversary activity, evidence needs, and reversibility.
learningObjectives: differentiate short-term and sustained containment
evaluate isolation options and side effects
define containment verification steps
document decision rationale and residual risk

notes.text: Containment reduces the adversary’s ability to continue harmful activity. The best action depends on the incident: disabling a user, isolating an endpoint, blocking a network path, restricting cloud permissions, or temporarily taking a service offline can each be appropriate under different conditions.

items: Containment should be authorized and coordinated with service owners when feasible.
Prioritize stopping ongoing harm and preventing lateral movement or data loss.
Consider whether the action destroys volatile evidence or changes the adversary’s behavior.
After containment, verify that the expected risk reduction actually occurred.

practicals.title: Choose containment actions
practicals.description: Evaluate three incident scenarios and select immediate, secondary, and verification actions.
steps: For an active credential compromise, select identity containment and verification.
For a malware-infected workstation, select endpoint/network containment and verification.
For a compromised cloud account, select access and resource containment.
For each, document business impact and evidence-preservation considerations.
practicals.solution: Choose actions that are fast, proportionate, and reversible where possible, but prioritize preventing continued harm when the risk is high.
practicals.output: Each scenario has a documented containment decision, rationale, owner, and verification step.

quiz.question: What should follow a containment action?
options: Assume it worked
Verify that the relevant malicious activity or access path is actually blocked
Delete the case
Stop collecting evidence
quiz.answer: Verify that the relevant malicious activity or access path is actually blocked
quiz.explanation: Containment is an action whose effectiveness must be validated with appropriate telemetry.

summary: Containment is a risk decision with technical and business consequences.
Every containment action should have an expected effect and a verification method.

lessons.title: Eradication and Root-Cause Analysis
lessons.description: Remove persistence and contributing weaknesses while distinguishing immediate cleanup from durable remediation.
learningObjectives: define eradication criteria
identify persistence and enabling conditions
avoid declaring eradication based only on symptom disappearance
connect root cause to corrective actions

notes.text: Eradication removes the cause or mechanisms of continued compromise. Root-cause analysis asks why the incident was possible and why detection or containment did not stop it earlier. Root cause should be evidence-backed; “user clicked a link” may be an initial action, but the investigation may also reveal credential reuse, missing MFA, excessive privilege, or inadequate monitoring.

items: Remove malicious persistence or unauthorized access mechanisms.
Correct exploited vulnerabilities or misconfigurations.
Rotate or revoke exposed credentials and secrets as appropriate.
Validate that the attacker’s access path is gone.
Document residual risk and required follow-up improvements.

practicals.title: Create eradication acceptance criteria
practicals.description: Write acceptance criteria for declaring a compromised endpoint or account eradicated.
steps: Define what evidence must be absent or remediated.
Define credential/session reset requirements.
Define vulnerability or configuration remediation requirements.
Define post-eradication monitoring.
Include a condition for reopening the incident if malicious activity reappears.
practicals.solution: Make each criterion observable and testable. Avoid criteria such as “system looks clean.”
practicals.output: The result is a measurable eradication checklist that supports a defensible closure decision.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes root-cause analysis?
options: It is simply naming the malware.
It identifies the conditions and contributing factors that enabled or prolonged the incident.
It is performed only by law enforcement.
It replaces containment.
quiz.answer: It identifies the conditions and contributing factors that enabled or prolonged the incident.
quiz.explanation: Root-cause analysis connects observed compromise to enabling conditions and improvement opportunities.

summary: Eradication requires evidence-based acceptance criteria.
Root cause should explain enabling conditions, not merely label an observable symptom.

lessons.title: Ransomware and Data-Extortion Response
lessons.description: Respond to ransomware and data-extortion scenarios using isolation, evidence preservation, recovery priorities, and communications.
learningObjectives: recognize common response priorities in ransomware incidents
identify why backups and recovery evidence matter
preserve volatile evidence when practical and authorized
sequence containment, investigation, recovery, and communications

notes.text: CISA’s ransomware guidance recommends isolating impacted systems, prioritizing critical services, examining detection systems and logs, preserving relevant evidence, and restoring from offline or otherwise protected backups. It also emphasizes incident-response and communications planning before an incident.

Do not assume that paying a ransom guarantees recovery, removes the attacker, or resolves data-exposure risk. Organizational, legal, regulatory, insurance, and executive decisions require appropriate authority and current advice.

items: Treat a ransomware event as potentially broader than the encrypted systems.
Investigate precursor access and persistence.
Protect backups from attacker access and verify restoration paths.
Use clean recovery environments where appropriate.
Document decisions and notification assessments.

practicals.title: Run a ransomware tabletop
practicals.description: Execute a staged tabletop for a ransomware event affecting a file server and several endpoints.
steps: At T+0, declare the scenario and assign roles.
At T+15, add evidence of lateral movement and an administrator account compromise.
At T+30, add a backup-integrity question and a possible data-exfiltration signal.
At T+45, require a recovery priority decision and a communications update.
Capture decisions, owners, assumptions, and lessons learned.
practicals.solution: Use the CISA ransomware response checklist as a reference point, but adapt actions to the fictional organization’s approved plan and authorities.
practicals.output: The tabletop produces a decision log, updated incident scope, containment plan, recovery priority, and improvement backlog.

quiz.question: Why should a ransomware investigation consider precursor activity?
options: Ransomware always begins with a single known file.
The encryption event may be the final stage of an earlier compromise.
Precursor activity is irrelevant after encryption.
It guarantees attribution.
quiz.answer: The encryption event may be the final stage of an earlier compromise.
quiz.explanation: CISA notes that ransomware can be evidence of an earlier unresolved compromise; investigation should look for prior access and persistence.

summary: Ransomware response is both a technical containment problem and a recovery/communications problem.
Backups are useful only if they are protected, available, and restorable.

lessons.title: Secure Recovery and Reconnection
lessons.description: Restore services to a known-good state, validate security controls, and avoid reinfecting clean environments.
learningObjectives: define recovery entry and exit criteria
prioritize restoration by business criticality and dependencies
validate restored systems before reconnecting them
capture lessons learned during recovery

notes.text: Recovery is not simply “turn systems back on.” NIST SP 800-184 emphasizes recovery planning, exercises, stakeholder feedback, testing, documentation, and continuous improvement.

items: Confirm containment and eradication assumptions.
Select clean restoration sources and prioritize services.
Restore in an isolated or controlled environment when appropriate.
Validate identity, security controls, configurations, and telemetry.
Reconnect according to dependency and risk order.
Monitor closely and document deviations.

practicals.title: Create recovery gates
practicals.description: Design recovery gates for a compromised application server.
steps: Define prerequisites before restoration.
Define technical validation after restoration.
Define security telemetry that must be active before reconnecting.
Define business-owner acceptance criteria.
Define enhanced monitoring after reconnection.
practicals.solution: Think in gates: evidence and containment, clean build, validation, business acceptance, controlled reconnection, and heightened monitoring.
practicals.output: The gates provide a repeatable path from compromised state to monitored production state.

quiz.question: What is a strong recovery principle?
options: Restore first and investigate later
Reconnect only after defined technical and business validation criteria are met
Disable all logging during recovery
Assume backups are trustworthy without testing
quiz.answer: Reconnect only after defined technical and business validation criteria are met
quiz.explanation: Recovery should restore known-good operation while reducing the chance of reinfection or recurring compromise.

summary: Recovery should be staged, validated, and prioritized by mission impact and dependencies.
Recovery exercises reveal weaknesses before a real incident does.

tasks.title: Design a containment and recovery playbook
tasks.description: Create a scenario-based playbook for a compromised administrator account with suspected lateral movement.
tasks.problemStatement: The response team sees suspicious administrative logins, endpoint alerts, and a possible file-share compromise. Create a playbook that balances rapid containment with evidence preservation and recovery.
tasks.hint: For every action, specify why it is needed, who can authorize it, and how responders verify the result.
tasks.solutionCode:
playbook = [
    {"phase":"containment", "action":"restrict compromised administrator access", "verify":"new privileged sessions are blocked"},
    {"phase":"scoping", "action":"review identity, endpoint and file-share telemetry", "verify":"affected entities are recorded"},
    {"phase":"eradication", "action":"remove persistence and rotate exposed secrets", "verify":"persistence checks are clean"},
    {"phase":"recovery", "action":"restore validated systems in priority order", "verify":"security telemetry and service tests pass"},
]
for step in playbook:
    print(step)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution models a response as a set of decision-driven steps with explicit verification. A real playbook should add organizational approvals, evidence references, contacts, and tool-specific procedures.

modules.title: Digital Forensics, Evidence, and Reporting
modules.description: Learn the forensic process, evidence preservation, hashing, acquisition decisions, artifact analysis, chain-of-custody concepts, and defensible reporting.

lessons.title: Forensic Process in Incident Response
lessons.description: Apply the NIST forensic process of collection, examination, analysis, and reporting within an incident-response context.
learningObjectives: explain the four phases of the NIST forensic process
distinguish collection from analysis
identify when forensic preservation is necessary
document acquisition and handling decisions

items: Collection: identify, label, record, and collect relevant data while preserving integrity.
Examination: use appropriate tools and methods to extract relevant information while protecting integrity.
Analysis: interpret examined results to answer defined questions.
Reporting: document actions, findings, limitations, and recommendations.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-86 describes this four-phase process and emphasizes that the exact procedure should reflect organizational policies, legal requirements, and the type of investigation.

practicals.title: Design a forensic collection plan
practicals.description: Create a collection plan for a compromised workstation and identity account.
steps: Define investigation questions.
List volatile and non-volatile evidence sources.
Prioritize evidence by volatility, relevance, and retention risk.
Define integrity and documentation controls.
Define the handoff from collection to examination and analysis.
practicals.solution: Start with investigative questions and work backward to the evidence required to answer them.
practicals.output: The plan identifies evidence sources, priorities, integrity controls, and analysis questions.

quiz.question: Which sequence matches the NIST SP 800-86 forensic process?
options: Analysis, collection, reporting, examination
Collection, examination, analysis, reporting
Reporting, recovery, collection, detection
Containment, eradication, collection, recovery
quiz.answer: Collection, examination, analysis, reporting
quiz.explanation: NIST SP 800-86 describes collection, examination, analysis, and reporting as its basic forensic process.

summary: Forensics should answer defined questions while preserving evidence integrity.
Collection and analysis are distinct activities and should be documented separately.

lessons.title: Integrity, Hashing, and Chain of Custody
lessons.description: Use cryptographic hashes and handling records to support evidence integrity and reproducibility.
learningObjectives: explain what a cryptographic hash can and cannot establish
calculate a file hash using standard tools
design a simple evidence-handling record
identify chain-of-custody fields and limitations

notes.text: A cryptographic hash provides a fixed-length digest of data. If the same input is hashed with the same algorithm, the digest can be compared to detect changes. A hash does not by itself prove who created a file, who possessed it, or that the underlying acquisition process was lawful or complete.

Linux/macOS:
sha256sum evidence.bin

PowerShell:
Get-FileHash .\evidence.bin -Algorithm SHA256

items: Record the hash algorithm and resulting digest.
Record evidence identifier, source, acquisition time, collector, storage location, and transfer history as appropriate.
Preserve original evidence separately from working copies when required.
Use organizational procedures and legal guidance for evidentiary handling.

practicals.title: Hash and document an evidence file
practicals.description: Create a SHA-256 hash record for a sample file and document the handling event.
steps: Create or select a non-sensitive sample file.
Calculate its SHA-256 digest using a standard tool.
Record the file identifier, hash algorithm, digest, timestamp, operator role, and storage location.
Copy the file and verify the copy hash matches.
Explain what the matching hash does and does not prove.
practicals.solution: Use SHA-256 for the exercise and keep the original and working copy clearly identified.
practicals.output: The original and copy produce the same SHA-256 digest, and the case record explains the integrity comparison.

quiz.question: What does a matching SHA-256 hash primarily demonstrate?
options: The file is safe
The two hashed byte sequences are consistent with being identical under SHA-256
The file was created by a specific person
The acquisition was legally authorized
quiz.answer: The two hashed byte sequences are consistent with being identical under SHA-256
quiz.explanation: A matching digest supports integrity comparison but does not establish provenance, legality, or safety.

summary: Hashing supports integrity verification but is not a complete chain-of-custody process.
Evidence handling should be documented from acquisition through analysis and storage.

lessons.title: Windows, Linux, and Cloud Artifacts
lessons.description: Select platform-specific artifacts for investigation without assuming every artifact is available or equally reliable.
learningObjectives: identify high-value Windows artifacts
identify high-value Linux artifacts
identify common cloud control-plane and identity artifacts
evaluate artifact limitations and retention

items: Windows examples: Security/Application/System event logs, PowerShell operational logs where configured, scheduled tasks, services, registry locations, Prefetch where available, browser artifacts, endpoint telemetry.
Linux examples: journald/syslog, authentication logs, systemd units, cron, shell history when relevant, process/socket state, package records.
Cloud examples: identity/authentication events, control-plane audit events, API activity, resource configuration changes, network-flow or load-balancer logs where enabled.

notes.text: Artifact availability varies by operating system, version, configuration, retention, and logging policy. Never state that an artifact must exist on every system.

practicals.title: Build an artifact-to-question matrix
practicals.description: Map investigation questions to platform artifacts and document limitations.
steps: Choose questions such as “Who logged in?”, “What executed?”, “What changed?”, and “What external destination was contacted?”
Map each question to Windows, Linux, and cloud sources where applicable.
Identify the source that would be most authoritative for each question in the fictional environment.
List one reason the evidence could be absent or incomplete.
practicals.solution: Treat each artifact as one evidence source among others; record configuration and retention dependencies.
practicals.output: The matrix links investigative questions to concrete artifacts and highlights evidence limitations.

quiz.question: Why should artifact availability be treated as conditional?
options: Operating systems never log events
Artifacts depend on configuration, version, retention, and collection coverage
Artifacts are always fake
Cloud systems cannot generate audit logs
quiz.answer: Artifacts depend on configuration, version, retention, and collection coverage
quiz.explanation: Forensic artifacts are environment-dependent and may be missing or altered by configuration and retention policies.

summary: Platform artifacts are evidence sources, not universal guarantees.
Investigators should document collection coverage and limitations.

lessons.title: Forensic Reporting and Executive-Technical Communication
lessons.description: Write reports that separate facts, analysis, confidence, limitations, and recommendations for different audiences.
learningObjectives: write a defensible incident finding
separate observed evidence from inference
communicate uncertainty without making the report unusable
tailor technical and executive summaries

items: Executive summary: what happened, impact, current status, and major decisions.
Scope and timeline: affected entities and important chronology.
Evidence and methods: what was collected and how.
Findings: facts and supported interpretations.
Limitations: missing logs, retention gaps, inaccessible systems, or uncertain attribution.
Actions: containment, eradication, recovery, and improvements.

notes.text: A strong report allows another qualified reviewer to understand the reasoning without reconstructing the entire investigation from raw data. It should distinguish facts from interpretations and avoid overstating confidence.

practicals.title: Write a two-audience incident report
practicals.description: Create an executive summary and a technical findings section for the same fictional incident.
steps: Write a five-sentence executive summary focused on impact, status, and decisions.
Write a technical findings section with evidence references and confidence.
List known limitations.
Write three corrective actions tied to observed root causes.
Check that the executive section does not contain unsupported technical conclusions.
practicals.solution: Use the same evidence base for both sections, but change vocabulary and detail rather than changing the underlying facts.
practicals.output: The report communicates consistent facts at two levels of detail and makes uncertainty visible.

quiz.question: Which reporting practice is strongest?
options: Present every hypothesis as fact
Hide evidence gaps
Separate observed facts, analysis, confidence, and limitations
Use technical jargon for executives
quiz.answer: Separate observed facts, analysis, confidence, and limitations
quiz.explanation: This structure makes the report more defensible and useful to both technical reviewers and decision makers.

summary: Incident reports should be evidence-backed, transparent about limitations, and audience-appropriate.
Confidence should track evidence quality rather than the analyst’s certainty alone.

tasks.title: Create a defensible evidence package
tasks.description: Build a small evidence package specification and report for a simulated endpoint incident.
tasks.problemStatement: Define evidence identifiers, hashes, collection records, analysis findings, and a concise final report. The deliverable must allow another analyst to understand what was collected and why.
tasks.hint: Start with the questions the investigation must answer; do not collect everything merely because it is available.
tasks.solutionCode:
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("evidence.bin")
sha256 = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
print({"file": path.name, "algorithm": "SHA-256", "digest": sha256})
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution demonstrates reproducible hashing using Python standard library. The complete assignment also requires a human-readable evidence register and report; hashing alone is not chain of custody.

modules.title: Communication, Coordination, Metrics, and Continuous Improvement
modules.description: Coordinate people and stakeholders, manage communications and notifications, measure response performance, and turn incidents into sustained improvements.

lessons.title: Incident Communications and Stakeholder Management
lessons.description: Design internal and external communication flows that are accurate, timely, authorized, and appropriate to uncertainty.
learningObjectives: define stakeholder groups and information needs
write a holding statement without unsupported claims
establish communication ownership and approval paths
manage updates during evolving incidents

items: Technical responders need actionable detail.
Executives need impact, decisions, risk, and next actions.
Employees may need safe instructions and reporting guidance.
Customers, regulators, partners, insurers, and law enforcement may have separate requirements.
A holding statement should avoid speculation and preserve room for investigation to evolve.

notes.text: Notification requirements vary by jurisdiction, sector, contract, data type, and incident circumstances. Incident-response training should teach escalation to qualified legal/privacy professionals rather than provide one universal deadline.

practicals.title: Draft an incident holding statement
practicals.description: Write a neutral holding statement for a suspected service compromise before scope is fully known.
steps: State that an investigation is underway.
State confirmed service impact without speculating about the attacker.
Provide safe user actions if needed.
Identify where updates will be issued.
Have the statement reviewed against the fictional approval path.
practicals.solution: Avoid naming a cause, attacker, affected data, or number of affected users unless the case evidence has established it.
practicals.output: The statement is accurate under uncertainty and does not create unsupported commitments.

quiz.question: What is the safest approach when incident scope is uncertain?
options: Invent a precise number to reassure stakeholders
State what is confirmed, what is under investigation, and when/how updates will occur
Remain silent indefinitely
Publish raw forensic evidence
quiz.answer: State what is confirmed, what is under investigation, and when/how updates will occur
quiz.explanation: Accurate uncertainty management avoids speculation while keeping stakeholders informed.

summary: Communication is part of response, not an afterthought.
Legal and regulatory decisions should be escalated to appropriate specialists.

lessons.title: Metrics, Severity, and Response Performance
lessons.description: Measure response capability using meaningful operational metrics rather than vanity counts.
learningObjectives: define useful incident-response metrics
distinguish detection, response, containment, and recovery timing
interpret metrics without creating harmful incentives
use metrics to identify process bottlenecks

items: MTTD can describe time from relevant activity or event to detection, but the exact measurement definition must be standardized.
MTTA can describe time from alert/incident creation to acknowledgement.
MTTC can describe time to containment; define the containment endpoint explicitly.
MTTR is ambiguous unless the organization defines what “resolved” or “recovered” means.
Quality measures can include evidence completeness, playbook adherence, recurrence, and exercise findings.

notes.text: Metrics become misleading when definitions change between incidents. Document start/end conditions and exclusions.

practicals.title: Define an IR metrics dictionary
practicals.description: Create precise definitions for five response metrics.
steps: Choose five metrics spanning detection, acknowledgement, containment, recovery, and quality.
Define start event, end event, exclusions, data source, owner, and reporting cadence.
Give one example calculation using fictional timestamps.
Identify one way each metric could create an undesirable incentive.
practicals.solution: Define the measurement before calculating it. A metric without a stable definition cannot support meaningful trend analysis.
practicals.output: The dictionary makes response performance measurable and reviewable.

quiz.question: Why should metric definitions be explicit?
options: To make reports longer
Because the same metric name can otherwise hide different start/end conditions
Because metrics are never useful
To avoid collecting timestamps
quiz.answer: Because the same metric name can otherwise hide different start/end conditions
quiz.explanation: Explicit definitions make trends comparable and prevent misleading performance claims.

summary: Metrics should drive learning and capability improvement, not reward superficial speed.
Stable definitions are essential for trend analysis.

lessons.title: Lessons Learned, Exercises, and Maturity Improvement
lessons.description: Turn incidents and exercises into prioritized improvements and verify that changes actually work.
learningObjectives: conduct a blameless lessons-learned review
identify systemic improvements from incident evidence
design an exercise with measurable objectives
track corrective actions to closure

notes.text: NIST recovery guidance emphasizes exercises, debriefs, lessons learned, and continuous improvement. Improvement should connect observed problems to owners, remediation, validation, and residual risk.

items: What happened?
What did the team expect?
Where did reality differ?
What evidence supports the gap?
What change will reduce recurrence or impact?
How will the change be tested?
Who owns the change and by when?

practicals.title: Run a mini lessons-learned review
practicals.description: Analyze a fictional incident and produce an improvement backlog.
steps: Identify three process or technology gaps.
For each gap, describe impact and evidence.
Create a corrective action with owner, due date, and validation test.
Prioritize actions by risk reduction and effort.
Define how the organization will confirm the action remains effective.
practicals.solution: Do not write “train staff” as a complete corrective action. Specify the behavior or capability to change and how it will be tested.
practicals.output: The backlog contains measurable corrective actions linked to evidence and validation.

quiz.question: What makes a lessons-learned action strong?
options: It has no owner
It says “improve security”
It is tied to an observed gap and includes a validation method
It is deleted after the meeting
quiz.answer: It is tied to an observed gap and includes a validation method
quiz.explanation: Improvements need ownership and verification to become durable capability changes.

summary: Lessons learned should become tracked, testable improvements.
Exercises validate response capabilities before a real crisis does.

lessons.title: Information Sharing and Case Closure
lessons.description: Close incidents consistently, preserve useful knowledge, and share indicators or lessons when authorized and beneficial.
learningObjectives: define incident closure criteria
preserve the final case record and evidence references
identify useful information for internal or external sharing
distinguish closure from the end of all remediation work

notes.text: Closure should occur when defined response objectives are met and the incident can move to normal operational tracking. Some corrective actions may remain open as separate improvement work.

items: Closure should confirm scope, containment/eradication status, recovery status, residual risk, and required follow-up.
Preserve final timeline, findings, decisions, evidence inventory, and communications.
Share indicators or lessons only under applicable policy, legal, privacy, contractual, and information-sharing rules.
Use closure data to improve playbooks and future detection.

practicals.title: Create a closure checklist
practicals.description: Design a final incident-closure checklist that a responder can complete before closure.
steps: Confirm incident scope and affected assets.
Confirm containment and eradication criteria.
Confirm recovery and monitoring.
Confirm evidence and case documentation.
Confirm notification/communication status.
Create follow-up improvement records and residual-risk notes.
practicals.solution: Make every checklist item verifiable and include an owner for open follow-up actions.
practicals.output: The checklist provides a consistent closure gate and prevents premature case closure.

quiz.question: Does incident closure mean every improvement action is finished?
options: Always
No; response can close while tracked remediation continues separately
Only if the incident was minor
Only for cloud incidents
quiz.answer: No; response can close while tracked remediation continues separately
quiz.explanation: Closure should indicate that response objectives are met; longer-term improvements can remain tracked as follow-up work.

summary: Closure is a controlled transition from active response to normal improvement and risk management.
Useful case knowledge should be retained and shared according to authorization and policy.

tasks.title: Build an incident communications and improvement package
tasks.description: Create a communications plan, metrics dictionary, and lessons-learned backlog for a simulated data-exposure incident.
tasks.problemStatement: The incident is contained but the organization has incomplete information about the exact records accessed. Create materials that keep stakeholders informed without speculation and convert response gaps into measurable improvements.
tasks.hint: Keep facts, uncertainty, and commitments clearly separated.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The code is only a compact representation of the package structure. The student must provide actual definitions, text, ownership, and validation criteria.

modules.title: Cloud Incident Response, Automation, and Capstone
modules.description: Apply incident-response principles to cloud environments, automate safe evidence and triage workflows, and complete a realistic end-to-end incident-response capstone.

lessons.title: Cloud Incident Response and Shared Responsibility
lessons.description: Adapt incident-response methods to cloud identity, control-plane, workload, and service-provider boundaries.
learningObjectives: explain why cloud incident response still requires preparation and logging
identify cloud control-plane and identity evidence
apply shared-responsibility reasoning to incident scope
design a cloud containment decision

notes.text: Cloud incident response retains the core investigative principles of traditional response but changes the evidence and control surfaces. Cloud audit logs, identity events, resource configuration, API activity, provider telemetry, and account structure can become central evidence sources.

items: Know which security controls and logs are customer-controlled versus provider-controlled.
Centralize security-relevant logs where appropriate and protect them from unauthorized deletion.
Prepare emergency access and containment roles before incidents.
Use clean-room or isolated investigation environments when supported by the platform.

notes.text: AWS guidance, for example, recommends establishing an incident-response team and plan, centralizing relevant security findings/logs, and preparing containment and recovery workflows. The exact services differ by cloud provider, so students should map principles to their provider documentation.

practicals.title: Design a cloud IR evidence map
practicals.description: Create a cloud evidence map for compromised credentials and unauthorized resource changes.
steps: Identify identity events, control-plane events, network/service logs, and affected resource metadata.
Identify where the logs are stored and who can access them.
Define containment actions for the compromised identity and affected resources.
Define evidence-retention and integrity considerations.
Identify one provider boundary where the organization may need provider support.
practicals.solution: Separate customer-controlled evidence from provider-controlled evidence and document the escalation path for provider-side data.
practicals.output: The map provides a cloud-specific investigation and containment plan.

quiz.question: What is a key cloud IR preparation principle?
options: Assume the provider owns every response action
Prepare access, logging, evidence retrieval, and containment workflows before an incident
Disable cloud audit logs to reduce cost
Treat control-plane activity as irrelevant
quiz.answer: Prepare access, logging, evidence retrieval, and containment workflows before an incident
quiz.explanation: Cloud response depends heavily on prepared visibility and access to the control surfaces that responders will need during an incident.

summary: Cloud response requires explicit understanding of provider/customer control boundaries.
Control-plane and identity telemetry can be as important as workload telemetry.

lessons.title: Safe Automation for Incident Response
lessons.description: Design small automations that enrich and document response without creating uncontrolled destructive actions.
learningObjectives: distinguish enrichment automation from containment automation
design idempotent, auditable response actions
include approval and safety gates for high-impact actions
log automation inputs, decisions, and outcomes

notes.text: Automation can reduce repetitive work, but response automation should be designed around authorization, scope, reversibility, observability, and failure handling. A script that disables an account or isolates a host without validation can amplify an incident.

items: Enrichment: parse indicators, normalize timestamps, query approved data sources.
Decision support: score or group evidence while preserving analyst review.
Controlled action: execute approved containment with explicit scope and logging.
Recovery automation should include validation gates and rollback where feasible.

practicals.title: Build a safe IOC enrichment script
practicals.description: Create a Python script that reads indicators from a CSV, normalizes them, removes duplicates, and produces a review queue without contacting external systems.
steps: Create a CSV with indicator type, value, source, and timestamp.
Normalize whitespace and indicator type values.
Deduplicate indicators while preserving source references.
Output a JSON review queue.
Add validation that rejects empty or unsupported indicator types.
practicals.output: The script only normalizes and prepares evidence for review. It intentionally does not block traffic, delete files, disable accounts, or query third-party systems. This separation reduces automation risk.

quiz.question: Which automation design is safest for a first implementation?
options: Unreviewed destructive actions across all assets
Evidence enrichment with clear logs and human approval before high-impact actions
A script that deletes all matching files
An automation that hides its actions
quiz.answer: Evidence enrichment with clear logs and human approval before high-impact actions
quiz.explanation: Low-risk enrichment is easier to validate; high-impact containment should have authorization, scope, logging, and safety controls.

summary: Automation should improve consistency without hiding decisions or creating uncontrolled blast radius.
Start with enrichment and auditable workflows before high-impact automated containment.

lessons.title: Capstone Preparation: End-to-End Incident Workflow
lessons.description: Prepare for the final project by integrating detection, triage, scoping, containment, evidence, recovery, communication, and improvement into one case workflow.
learningObjectives: construct an end-to-end response workflow
define evidence and decision checkpoints
integrate technical and organizational response actions
prepare a final incident report and improvement backlog

notes.text: The capstone should be treated as a real incident case, not a collection of disconnected exercises. Students must maintain a single case narrative, evidence register, timeline, decision log, response actions, recovery record, and lessons-learned backlog.

items: Start with an alert or report and establish incident status.
Build scope from evidence rather than assumption.
Contain according to current risk and verify containment.
Preserve relevant evidence and maintain an auditable record.
Recover through defined gates and confirm monitoring.
Close with a report, metrics, and improvement actions.
